<details>
<summary>Click to reveal: where does the cube come from?</summary>
<p>Two facts multiply together.</p>
<p><b>1. Ties delete exactly the within-block variance.</b> If the response is constant on
each block of a partition, split the predictor into its block averages
<code>E[X|b]</code> plus a residual. The residual is orthogonal to every function of the
block label — that is the defining property of conditional expectation — so the
law of total variance gives <code>Var X = Var(E[X|b]) + W</code>, where <code>W</code>
is the within-block sum of squares. Cauchy–Schwarz on the surviving part yields
<code>rho^2 ≤ 1 − W/Var X</code>. Nothing is wasted here: taking the response to
be <code>E[X|b]</code> itself turns the inequality into an equality, so the ceiling is
<em>attained</em>.</p>
<p><b>2. Rank vectors cannot huddle.</b> A rank vector takes distinct integer values,
and <em>m</em> distinct integers are least spread out when they are consecutive. The spread
of <em>m</em> consecutive integers about their mean is exactly <code>(m^3 − m)/12</code>.
A block of <em>m</em> consecutive ranks has extent ~<em>m</em>, squared deviation ~<em>m</em>²
per point, and <em>m</em> points: total ~<em>m</em>³. The whole sample gives ~<em>n</em>³.
The ratio is <em>q</em>³.</p>
<p>Multiply: <code>rho^2 ≤ 1 − (m^3−m)/(n^3−n) ≈ 1 − q^3</code>.
Because variance is quadratic in a linear extent and the point count is itself linear,
the exponent is 3 and not 1. That single exponent is the whole story: at
<em>q</em> = 0.16 intuition expects a 16% penalty and reality delivers 0.4%.</p>
</details>

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal: why isotropic noise needs so much more than the floor</summary>
<p>The budget <code>Var(D) ≥ (a−b)^2 (n^3−n)/12</code> is a
<em>necessary</em> condition. It is attained only when the displacement <code>D</code> is
aligned with the dial — every unit of noise energy aimed squarely at cancelling the
signal.</p>
<p>Real estimator noise is not aimed. If <code>D</code> is independent of the dial, the
covariance <code>Cov(X, measured) = Cov(X, true)</code> is unchanged and only the
denominator inflates, so the score is attenuated by
<code>sqrt(V/(V+S))</code> with <code>V = (n^3−n)/12</code> the rank variance
and <code>S = Var(D)</code>. Solving for the observed attenuation
<code>b/a = 0.405/0.55 = 0.736</code> gives <code>S/V = 0.844</code>, i.e. an RMS
displacement of about 318 positions — roughly 40x the energy floor.</p>
<p>Both numbers point the same way. The floor is a theorem; the 318 is a model. Whichever
you use, the noise required dwarfs anything ties can produce.</p>
</details>

  "interactive_layout": "# The Cubic Wall: Why Coarse Data Barely Hurts a Rank Correlation

*A guided tour of tie ceilings, quantization ceilings, and noise budgets — and of a
diagnosis that turned out to be arithmetically impossible.*

---

## 1. A number that looked like a verdict

Somewhere in a large computational experiment sits a small object called a **dial**: a
cheap statistic $T(N)$ you can compute about an integer $N$, meant to predict something
expensive — the *smooth-hit rate* of a sieve run on $N$. If the dial is good, the moduli
it ranks highest really are the ones the sieve likes best, and you can spend your compute
where it pays.

You grade a dial with **Spearman's rank correlation**. Throw away the numbers, keep the
ordering: sort the $n$ sampled moduli by $T$, sort them again by measured rate, and ask
how well the two orderings agree. A score of $\rho = 1$ is perfect, $\rho = 0$ is
worthless. The project called a dial healthy if $\rho$ landed in $[0.55,\,0.85]$.

At bit length 56, with $n = 1200$ moduli, the number came back at

$$\rho = 0.405.$$

Below the band. And there was an obvious culprit right there in the log: the sieve was
**starved**. The mean smooth rate had collapsed to $0.89\%$, and **194 of the 1200 moduli
recorded zero hits**. Zero hits means the measured rate is literally the same number —
zero — for all 194. In rank terms, an enormous **tie block**. The recorded explanation
wrote itself: *the starved regime destroys rank resolution*.

It is a satisfying story. This page is about why it is arithmetically impossible.

> **The question nobody asked.** Not *does* a tie block hurt, but *how much*? Given that
> 194 of 1200 responses are tied, what is the highest score any dial in the universe could
> still achieve?

---

2. To reach the band edge $0.55$ by ties alone you need $q \approx 0.887$ — **almost nine
   tenths of the sample tied together**.
3. A jitter of a few hundred rank positions does more damage than either.

Everything else on this page explains why.

---

## 3. Where the cube comes from

The ceiling is not a heuristic. It is an exact theorem, and it is the product of two
independent facts.

### Fact one: ties delete a specific chunk of your predictor

Suppose the response $Y$ is constant on each block of a partition — that is exactly what
"tied" means. Then $Y$ cannot see any variation of the predictor *inside* a block. Split
the predictor $X$ into its **block averages** $\mathbb{E}[X\mid b]$ (the coarse picture)
plus a residual $X - \mathbb{E}[X\mid b]$ (everything happening inside blocks).

The residual is orthogonal to every function of the block label. That is the defining
property of conditional expectation, and it gives the
[law of total variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_total_variance):

$$\operatorname{Var}X \;=\; \operatorname{Var}\big(\mathbb{E}[X\mid b]\big) \;+\; W,
\qquad W = \sum_i \big(X_i - \mathbb{E}[X\mid b]_i\big)^2 .$$

Against a blockwise-constant response, that $W$ is **dead weight**. Applying
[Cauchy–Schwarz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Schwarz_inequality) to the
surviving part gives:

> **Tie-Block Ceiling.** If $Y$ is constant on each block of the partition $b$, then for
> *every* predictor $X$,
> $$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2 \;\le\; \big(\operatorname{Var}X - W\big)\cdot\operatorname{Var}Y,
> \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \rho(X,Y)^2 \;\le\; 1 - \frac{W}{\operatorname{Var}X}.$$

You are penalised exactly and only for the resolution the measurement threw away.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal:</b> is Cauchy–Schwarz throwing away most of the truth?</summary>

This is the first objection anyone raises, and it deserves a real answer: perhaps the
*true* ceiling is far lower and the inequality is lossy.

It is not. There is a **Sharpness Theorem**: the ceiling is *attained*, and the response
that attains it is the block-averaged predictor $\mathbb{E}[X\mid b]$ itself.

The proof is two short computations. First, block averaging preserves the mean (take
$h \equiv 1$ in the orthogonality relation), so by the law of total variance
$\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid b]) = \operatorname{Var}X - W$. Second,
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, \mathbb{E}[X\mid b]) = \operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid b])$,
because when you expand the covariance the cross term is again an orthogonality instance
and vanishes. Substituting one into the other turns the inequality into an equality.

Geometrically: $\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\mid b]$ is the **orthogonal projection** onto the space
of blockwise-constant functions. The best blockwise-constant response to correlate with
$X$ is the projection of $X$ itself, and it achieves precisely the projected norm. So
$\operatorname{Var}X - W$ is not an upper estimate of the achievable numerator — it *is*
the achievable numerator.
</details>

### Fact two: rank vectors cannot huddle

So how big is $W$ for a *rank* vector? Rank vectors are special: they take **distinct
integer values**. And $m$ distinct integers cannot be crowded together — the tightest they
can possibly pack is consecutively. The spread of $m$ consecutive integers about their
mean is exactly

$$\frac{m^3 - m}{12}.$$

> **Discrete Spread Bound.** Any $m$ distinct integers have squared spread at least
> $(m^3-m)/12$, with equality precisely for a consecutive run.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal:</b> the proof of the spread bound</summary>

Three steps.

**Step 1 — go pairwise.** For any finite collection,
$$\sum_i\sum_j (x_i - x_j)^2 = 2|s|\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2 .$$
So the spread about the mean and the mean pairwise squared distance are the same object up
to a factor $2|s|$. The pairwise form is what we can compare across configurations.

**Step 2 — monotone integer sequences expand.** Enumerate your $m$ distinct integers in
increasing order as $f(0) < f(1) < \cdots < f(m-1)$. Then $a \mapsto f(a) - a$ is monotone,
because a single step increases $f$ by at least 1 (strictly increasing integers) and
increases $a$ by exactly 1. Hence $f(b) - f(a) \ge b - a$ for $a \le b$, and squaring,
$(f(a)-f(c))^2 \ge (a-c)^2$ for *every* pair.

**Step 3 — compute the model.** For the consecutive configuration $x_a = a$, using
$\sum_{a<m} a = m(m-1)/2$ and $\sum_{a<m} a^2 = m(m-1)(2m-1)/6$,
$$\sum_a\sum_c (a-c)^2 = \frac{m(m^3-m)}{6}.$$

Combine: the pairwise sum of your configuration dominates the model's, termwise, so it is
at least $m(m^3-m)/6$; dividing by $2m$ converts back to centred form and gives
$(m^3-m)/12$. Equality in step 2 for all pairs forces $f(a)-f(c) = a-c$, i.e. consecutive
values.

This is a **discrete isoperimetric inequality**: among all $m$-element integer
configurations, the consecutive run minimises spread.
</details>

### Multiply them together

Applied to the whole sample, the spread bound is an identity: a rank vector on $n$ points
has variance exactly $(n^3-n)/12$. Applied to a tie block of size $m$, it lower-bounds the
dead weight by $(m^3-m)/12$. Divide:

$$\boxed{\ \rho^2 \;\le\; 1 - \frac{m^3-m}{n^3-n} \;\approx\; 1 - q^3, \qquad q = \frac{m}{n}.\ }$$

**The tie penalty is cubic in the tie fraction.** That is the whole story.

Why cubic and not linear? Variance is a *quadratic* functional of a *linear* extent, and
the number of contributing points scales with the block size too. A block of $m$
consecutive ranks has extent $\sim m$, squared deviation $\sim m^2$ per point, and $m$
points: total $\sim m^3$. The whole sample gives $\sim n^3$. Ratio: $q^3$.

At $q = 0.16$, intuition expects a 16% penalty. Reality delivers 0.4%. That factor of 40
is what the picture below makes visceral.

## 4. Two escape routes, both closed

A good sceptic offers two rescues. We have already closed the first (the ceiling is
attained — see the hidden proof above). Here is the second.

> **"Maybe it's not one block — it's the whole grid of them."**

A rate is a *count* divided by a *trial budget*, so the measured response is **quantized**:
it takes only $r$ distinct values, and every level is a tie block of its own. Surely the
whole partition does more damage than the single zero block?

The ceiling generalises: every block $k$ of size $m_k$ subtracts its own
$(m_k^3 - m_k)/12$. (Pleasingly, this *derives* the classical Spearman tie correction
rather than assuming it.) And then a
[power-mean inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_mean) finishes the job:
subject to $\sum_k m_k = n$, the quantity $\sum_k m_k^3$ is **minimised** when all $r$
blocks are equally populated, giving $\sum_k m_k^3 \ge n^3/r^2$. So:

> **Quantization Ceiling.** If the response takes at most $r$ distinct values, then
> $$\rho^2 \;\le\; 1 - \frac{n^3/r^2 - n}{n^3-n} \;\xrightarrow[\;n\to\infty\;]{}\; 1 - \frac{1}{r^2}.$$

And here is the kicker. For every $r \ge 2$ this is at least $3/4$, so $\rho \le 0.866$ at
worst. **Even a response quantized to two levels — one single bit of information per
sample point — permits a rank correlation of 0.866.**

The verdict is total: one block, the whole partition, or maximally brutal quantization —
*no tie-based mechanism whatsoever* can push the score below the band. Go back to the
widget and try the **Binary quantization** preset to see it.

## 5. So what actually happened?

If ties didn't do it, what did? There is exactly one candidate left, and it is the one that
creates **no ties at all**.

At a $0.89\%$ smooth rate, the "measured rate" of each modulus is not the rate — it is a
Monte-Carlo estimate from a finite budget of trials. And a noisy estimate does not tie
things together; it **shuffles** them. Every modulus still gets its own distinct rank; they
are just in the wrong places.

How much shuffling would that take? The answer comes from reading a stability theorem
*backwards*. Covariance is linear in its second argument, so

$$\big(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) - \operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)\big)^2 \;\le\; \operatorname{Var}X\cdot\operatorname{Var}(Y-Z).$$

Forwards, that says correlation is robust: perturb the response a little, move the score a
little. **Backwards, it says a large drop in the score is a certificate of a large
perturbation.**

> **Noise Budget.** If a dial scores at least $a$ against the *true* response ranking but
> only $b \le a$ against the *measured* one, then the displacement $D$ (measured rank minus
> true rank) satisfies
> $$\operatorname{Var}(D) \;\ge\; (a-b)^2\,\frac{n^3-n}{12}.$$

Instantiate at the recorded numbers. Suppose the dial is genuinely a band-edge dial, worth
$a = 0.55$ against the truth, and measured $b = 0.405$, with $n = 1200$:

$$\operatorname{Var}(D) \;\ge\; (0.145)^2\cdot\frac{1200^3-1200}{12} \;\approx\; 3.0\times10^6,$$

which is an RMS displacement of about **50 rank positions out of 1200** — some $4\%$ of the
sample, for every modulus, on average.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal:</b> why 50 is only the floor, and isotropic noise needs ~318</summary>

The budget is a *necessary* condition, not a sufficient one, and it is attained only when
the displacement is **adversarially aligned** — every unit of noise energy aimed squarely
at cancelling this particular dial.

Real estimator noise is not aimed. If the displacement is independent of the dial, then
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, \text{measured}) = \operatorname{Cov}(X, \text{true})$ is unchanged
and only the denominator inflates, so the score is attenuated by

$$\frac{b}{a} = \sqrt{\frac{V}{V+S}}, \qquad V = \frac{n^3-n}{12}, \quad S = \operatorname{Var}(D).$$

Solving at $(a,b) = (0.55, 0.405)$ gives $S/V = (a/b)^2 - 1 = 0.844$, hence
$\operatorname{Var}(D) \approx 1.22\times10^8$ — an RMS displacement of about **318 rank
positions, 27% of the sample**, roughly $40\times$ the certified energy floor.

The two numbers bracket the truth: the floor is a theorem, the 318 is a model. Whichever
you use, the required noise is *enormous*, while the entire 194-point tie block costs
$0.002$. The conclusion only hardens.
</details>

This algorithm packages the certificate, and inverts it into a design rule — how accurate
must the response measurement be for the score to stay in band?

## 7. What the floor really is

The original headline said the dial's bit-length stability "has a practical floor near bit
length 54, beyond which the starved regime destroys rank resolution." Half of that
survives — and the surviving half is sharper than the original.

The floor is real: past some bit length the dial does leave the band. But:

- It is **not a rank-resolution phenomenon.** Resolution loss costs $q^3$, and $q^3$ is
  negligible at the observed starvation.
- It is a property of the **measurement apparatus**, not of the dial. The dial may be
  perfectly serviceable at bit length 56; the experiment simply lacks the accuracy to
  grade it.
- It has an **explicit location**: where the Monte-Carlo error of the rate estimate, in
  rank units, reaches roughly $(a - b)/\sqrt{12}$ of the sample size — here about $4\%$.

So the floor moves with the **trial budget**, not with the bit length as such. Bit length
enters only through the smooth rate, which controls the estimator variance.

And unlike the story it replaces, this one is **falsifiable**. Re-run the rate measurement
at bit length 56 with an independent seed and compare the two induced rankings. Rank
jitter far below 50 positions? Then noise fails too and something genuinely new is
happening. Jitter in the range 50–318? The diagnosis is confirmed and the remedy is
prescribed: raise the trial budget until the jitter fits the band.

---

## 8. The moral, which outlives the experiment

When a rank statistic degrades, the reflex is to blame **coarseness**: ties, quantization,
saturation, floor effects, censoring. Coarseness *feels* like it should be devastating. But
the cube says otherwise.

| Mechanism at $n = 1200$ | Damage |
|---|---|
| Tie 194 of 1200 points (16%) into one block | $\rho \le 0.9979$ |
| Quantize the response to 10 levels | $\rho \le 0.995$ |
| Quantize the response to **2** levels | $\rho \le 0.866$ |
| Displace ranks by $\approx 318$ positions (27%), independently | $\rho$ drops by $0.145$ |

**Rank correlation is astonishingly tolerant of coarseness and astonishingly intolerant of
jitter.** Coarse data is usually fine; wrong data is not. The two failure modes look
identical in a log file and are separated by a cube.

None of the mathematics here is exotic. The law of total variance is a century old;
Cauchy–Schwarz is older; that consecutive integers minimise spread is an exercise. The tie
correction $(m^3-m)/12$ appears in
[Spearman's own tables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spearman%27s_rank_correlation_coefficient).
What was missing was nobody having multiplied it out.

That is the trade this analysis bought: a comfortable story, exchanged for an
uncomfortable, checkable one.

`0.89 %` smooth rate the measured rate for each modulus is a Monte-Carlo estimate,

namespace TieCeiling

open Finset

variable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]

/-! ## Bilinearity -/

lemma mean_sub (Y Z : ι → ℝ) : mean (fun i => Y i - Z i) = mean Y - mean Z := by
  rw [mean, mean, mean, Finset.sum_sub_distrib, sub_div]

/-- Covariance is additive in the second argument. -/
lemma cov_sub_right (X Y Z : ι → ℝ) :
    cov X (fun i => Y i - Z i) = cov X Y - cov X Z := by
  rw [cov, cov, cov, mean_sub, ← Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun i _ => by ring

/-! ## The perturbation bound -/

/-- **Perturbing the response perturbs the covariance by at most the energy of the
perturbation.**  This is the quantitative statement that correlation is stable,
and read backwards it is a *lower bound on the noise* needed to destroy a
correlation. -/
theorem cov_diff_sq_le (X Y Z : ι → ℝ) :
    (cov X Y - cov X Z) ^ 2 ≤ varOf X * varOf (fun i => Y i - Z i) := by
  rw [← cov_sub_right X Y Z]
  exact cov_sq_le X (fun i => Y i - Z i)

/-! ## The noise budget for rank data -/

/-- **The noise budget.**  Let `X` be a dial's rank vector on `n` points, `Z` the
rank vector of the *true* response and `Y` that of the *measured* response.  If
the dial correlates at level `a` with the truth but only at level `b ≤ a` with the
measurement, then the measurement must have displaced the ranking with energy at
least `(a - b)² (n³ - n)/12`.

No tie hypothesis is used: this is the mechanism that operates *after* the tie
ceilings of cycles 1 and 2 have been shown not to bind. -/
theorem rank_displacement_energy_ge {n : ℕ} (σ τ υ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (a b : ℝ)

rank-resolution phenomenon at all.  Ties, whether concentrated in the zero-hit

producing it.  The residual must be *estimator noise*: at a `0.89 %` smooth rate

ranking, and permutation noise attenuates correlation without creating any ties.

variance of the rate estimator, not about the dial.

open Finset

/-! ## Objection 1: the ceiling is attained -/

variable {ι κ : Type*} [Fintype ι] [Fintype κ] [DecidableEq κ]

/-- The block averages have the same mean as the original variable. -/
lemma mean_condExp (X : ι → ℝ) (b : ι → κ) : mean (condExp X b) = mean X := by
  rw [mean, mean, sum_condExp]

blocks: the ceiling is optimal, not merely an upper bound. -/
theorem cov_sq_eq_explained_of_condExp (X : ι → ℝ) (b : ι → κ) :

    have h := var_eq_explained_add_residual X b

      simp only [condExp]

# The tie-block ceiling on rank correlation (T-DIAL-56, paper 178)

## Scientific context

Papers 175/178 study a *dial*: a real statistic `T(N)` that is supposed to predict
the smooth-hit `rate(N)` of a sieve run at a given bit length.  Quality is measured
by `Spearman(T, rate)`, and the target band is `[0.55, 0.85]`.  At bit length `56`

same number for all `194` of them — a **tie block**.

This file supplies the exact mathematics of that mechanism.  A tie block is a set
on which the response variable is constant; the predictor `T` still varies there,
and every bit of that variation is invisible to any correlation with the response.
The result is a *ceiling*: no matter how good the dial is, its correlation cannot
exceed a number determined by the tie structure alone.

## Mathematical content

Let `b : ι → κ` be a block labelling and let `Y` be constant on each block
(`Y = g ∘ b`).  Write `E[X|b]` for the block-averaging (conditional expectation)
operator.  The chain of results is:

  that `m` distinct integers are least spread out when they are consecutive.
* `spearman_ceiling_of_tie_block` — combining the two: for a rank vector `X` on
  `n` points and a response tied on a block of size `m`,

namespace TieCeiling

open Finset

/-! ## Centred moments -/

variable {ι κ : Type*} [Fintype ι]

/-- Arithmetic mean of `X` over the whole index type. -/
noncomputable def mean (X : ι → ℝ) : ℝ := (∑ i, X i) / (Fintype.card ι)

/-- Uncentred covariance (sum, not average — all statements are scale-free in it). -/
noncomputable def cov (X Y : ι → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i, (X i - mean X) * (Y i - mean Y)

/-- Uncentred variance. -/
noncomputable def varOf (X : ι → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i, (X i - mean X) ^ 2

lemma varOf_eq_cov (X : ι → ℝ) : varOf X = cov X X := by
  simp [varOf, cov, sq]

lemma varOf_nonneg (X : ι → ℝ) : 0 ≤ varOf X :=
  Finset.sum_nonneg fun _ _ => sq_nonneg _

/-! ## Block averaging (conditional expectation on the tie partition) -/

variable [Fintype κ] [DecidableEq κ]

/-- The block of index labelled `k`. -/
def fiber (b : ι → κ) (k : κ) : Finset ι := Finset.univ.filter (fun i => b i = k)

/-- The average of `X` over the block labelled `k` (zero on empty blocks). -/
noncomputable def blockAvg (X : ι → ℝ) (b : ι → κ) (k : κ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ i ∈ fiber b k, X i) / (fiber b k).card

/-- `E[X | b]`: the block-averaging operator. -/
noncomputable def condExp (X : ι → ℝ) (b : ι → κ) : ι → ℝ := fun i => blockAvg X b (b i)

omit [Fintype κ] in
lemma mem_fiber {b : ι → κ} {k : κ} {i : ι} : i ∈ fiber b k ↔ b i = k := by
  simp [fiber]

omit [Fintype κ] in
/-- The residual `X - E[X|b]` sums to zero over each block. -/
lemma sum_residual_fiber (X : ι → ℝ) (b : ι → κ) (k : κ) :
    ∑ i ∈ fiber b k, (X i - condExp X b i) = 0 := by
  rcases Finset.eq_empty_or_nonempty (fiber b k) with h | h

  · have hcard : ((fiber b k).card : ℝ) ≠ 0 :=

    rw [Finset.sum_sub_distrib, Finset.sum_congr rfl hconst, Finset.sum_const, nsmul_eq_mul,

    field_simp
    ring

lemma sum_residual_mul_comp (X : ι → ℝ) (b : ι → κ) (h : κ → ℝ) :

  refine Finset.sum_eq_zero ?_
  intro k _

    intro i hi

  rw [hfib, Finset.sum_congr rfl hk, ← Finset.mul_sum, sum_residual_fiber, mul_zero]

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic centred moments (uncentred sums, matching the theory's normalisation)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def mean(x: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Arithmetic mean of a finite sequence."""
    return sum(x) / len(x)


def var_of(x: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Uncentred variance: sum of squared deviations from the mean."""
    mx = mean(x)
    return sum((xi - mx) ** 2 for xi in x)


def cov(x: Sequence[float], y: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Uncentred covariance: sum of products of deviations."""
    mx, my = mean(x), mean(y)
    return sum((xi - mx) * (yi - my) for xi, yi in zip(x, y))


def pearson(x: Sequence[float], y: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Pearson correlation coefficient of two equal-length sequences."""
    vx, vy = var_of(x), var_of(y)
    if vx <= 0.0 or vy <= 0.0:
        return 0.0
    return cov(x, y) / math.sqrt(vx * vy)


def rank_vector(values: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """
    Midrank vector of `values`: ties receive the average of the ranks they
    would occupy. Ranks are 0-based.
    """
    n = len(values)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: values[i])
    ranks = [0.0] * n
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        j = i
        while j + 1 < n and values[order[j + 1]] == values[order[i]]:
            j += 1
        midrank = (i + j) / 2.0
        for k in range(i, j + 1):
            ranks[order[k]] = midrank
        i = j + 1
    return ranks


def spearman(x: Sequence[float], y: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Spearman rank correlation = Pearson correlation of the midranks."""
    return pearson(rank_vector(x), rank_vector(y))


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The theoretical quantities
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def spread_floor(m: int) -> float:
    """(m^3 - m)/12 — the sharp minimal spread of m distinct integers."""
    return (m**3 - m) / 12.0


def tie_block_ceiling(n: int, m: int) -> float:
    """
    Starved-Regime Ceiling: the largest Spearman coefficient achievable by
    any dial when m of the n responses are tied in a single block.
    """
    if n < 2:
        return 1.0
    ratio = (m**3 - m) / (n**3 - n)
    return math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - ratio))


def partition_ceiling(block_sizes: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """
    Full tie-partition ceiling: every block of size m_k subtracts its own
    (m_k^3 - m_k)/12 from the achievable numerator.
    """
    n = sum(block_sizes)
    if n < 2:
        return 1.0
    correction = sum(m**3 - m for m in block_sizes)
    return math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - correction / (n**3 - n)))


def quantization_ceiling(n: int, r: int) -> float:
    """
    Quantization Ceiling: the response takes at most r distinct values.
    Worst case (largest ceiling) is equally populated levels.
    """
    if n < 2 or r < 1:
        return 1.0
    ratio = (n**3 / r**2 - n) / (n**3 - n)
    return math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - ratio))


def starvation_threshold_fraction(rho_target: float) -> float:
    """
    Exact cubic threshold: the tie fraction q at which ties alone could
    force the Spearman coefficient down to rho_target (large-n limit).
    """
    return (1.0 - rho_target**2) ** (1.0 / 3.0)


def minimal_tie_block(n: int, rho_target: float) -> int:
    """
    Least integer m such that a tie block of size m could force
    rho <= rho_target at sample size n. Binary search, O(log n).
    """
    need = (1.0 - rho_target**2) * (n**3 - n)
    lo, hi = 1, n
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if mid**3 - mid >= need:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo


def noise_budget(a: float, b: float, n: int) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """
    Noise Budget. Returns (energy, rms) where
        energy = (a - b)^2 (n^3 - n)/12   is a certified lower bound on
                 Var(measured ranks - true ranks),
        rms    = sqrt(energy / n)         is the RMS rank displacement.
    """
    energy = (a - b) ** 2 * (n**3 - n) / 12.0
    return energy, math.sqrt(energy / n)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Conditional expectation on a block partition
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def cond_exp(x: Sequence[float], labels: Sequence[int]) -> List[float]:
    """E[x | labels]: replace each entry by the mean over its block."""
    sums: Dict[int, float] = {}
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for xi, k in zip(x, labels):
        sums[k] = sums.get(k, 0.0) + xi
        counts[k] = counts.get(k, 0) + 1
    return [sums[k] / counts[k] for k in labels]


def within_block_ss(x: Sequence[float], labels: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """W = sum_i (x_i - E[x | labels]_i)^2."""
    ce = cond_exp(x, labels)
    return sum((xi - ci) ** 2 for xi, ci in zip(x, ce))

concept.title: Uniqueness of the Two-Point Transreal Compactification
concept.concept_description:
The four-constructor carrier was topologised by fiat as EReal ⊔ {Φ}. We conjecture that this is forced: any compact Hausdorff topology making the finite fragment an open copy of the line and nullity isolated is that one. The approach is an ends argument for the real line inside a two-point remainder compactification.

If t is a compact Hausdorff topology on Transreal such that fin is an open embedding and {null} is open, then t equals the topology induced by the bijection Transreal ≃ EReal ⊕ Unit.

Formalise the end compactification of ℝ, show any compactification with two-point remainder of a two-ended locally compact space is the end compactification, then apply it to the complement of {null}.

All sharpness theorems about the division boundary become topology-canonical rather than model-dependent.

There is an exotic compact Hausdorff transreal topology; the guard's necessity would have to be re-examined in it.

            ## v19 Research Core Methodology — Speculative Scientific-Method Loop

You are the Principal Investigator leading a speculative research team with four
roles: **Hypothesizer**, **Experimenter**, **Analyst**, and **Critic**. This engine
is configured for **Speculative Specifying (Bold Conjectures)**: target high-risk,
high-reward, grand-challenge level research while maintaining adversarial rigor.

### Stage 1 — Hypothesize (team: Hypothesizer)
Brainstorm 5–7 falsifiable conjectures about the topic. At least three must be
bold, surprising, or grand-challenge level. Rank them by expected scientific
impact, not by ease of proof.
**CRITICAL SCORING REQUIREMENT**: To maximize your Phase A quality score, your
conjectures MUST aim for extreme `proof_depth` (deep structural hierarchies rather
than shallow one-liners) and `cross_domain` bridging (combining distinct areas of
math, e.g., algebra with topology, or geometry with combinatorics).

### Stage 2 — Experiment (team: Experimenter)
For each conjecture, attempt to prove it in Lean 4 or disprove it with a concrete
counterexample. Prioritize the boldest conjectures first. If a proof is beyond
reach, prove the strongest lemma you can and mark the remaining step with exactly
one `sorry` that is clearly documented.

### Stage 3 — Analyze (team: Analyst)
Summarize what survived, what failed, and **why** failures failed. Distinguish
"true but hard", "false", and "needs a different definition". Extract structural
patterns that could unify several observations.

### Stage 4 — Critique / Adversarial Review (team: Critic)
Before finalizing, challenge every theorem:
- Is any theorem trivial (True, definitional equality, `native_decide`)?
- Does every main theorem have 0 sorries?
- Do the results genuinely extend the attached catalog files?
- Are there hidden assumptions or corner cases that break the claim?
If you find a weakness, fix it or replace the theorem with a guarded version and
explain the boundary.

### Stage 5 — Synthesize (team: Principal Investigator)
Combine the verified results into clean, compiling Lean 4 files.
Write a `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` that lists 3–5 **bold, testable** conjectures
derived from Stage 3 and Stage 4. Each conjecture must include a
"The key insight is..." sentence and a "Why now?" justification.

ADDITIONALLY — machine-readable directions block (REQUIRED). In
FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md, after the prose sections, emit a fenced JSON
array named future_directions.json with one object per direction
(3–6 entries), each with exactly these keys:
```json
[{"title": "<short noun-phrase name, NOT a sentence>",
  "domain": "<one of: NumberTheory, Algebra, Geometry, Combinatorics, Computation, Physics, Probability, Cryptography, Logic, MachineLearning, Tropical, Bridges>",
  "description": "<2-4 sentences: the conjecture, the approach, why it matters>",
  "conjecture": "<the precise mathematical claim>",
  "test": "<how to test or formalize it>",
  "if_true": "<consequence if true>",
  "if_false": "<consequence if false>",
  "proof_strategy": "<sketch of the proof route>",
  "catalog_references": ["<Catalog.lean.module>"]}]

Titles must be noun phrases ("Silver-Ratio Spectral Gap for Pell Spines"),
never sentences or recaps ("This cycle proved..." is forbidden).

### Perpetual Scientific Iteration (do not stop at first synthesis)
When the research team comes together with results, do not stop. Treat the
synthesized findings as the next problem statement and immediately run the full
scientific-method loop again: hypothesize, experiment, review, synthesize,
critique. Repeat this cycle continuously within the available context window,
refining, deepening, and cross-checking until forced to emit output. Use
Aristotle to its fullest.

### Anti-Trivial Guardrails
- Do not produce trivial proofs (`True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `Inhabited X`-only, `native_decide`-only).
- Use an insight-bearing tactic (e.g. `induction`, `nlinarith`, `omega`, `field_simp`).

### Self-Critique Checklist
- No theorem is trivial.
- Every main theorem has 0 sorries.
- Lab Notes blocks contain real experimental data.

### Strictly Forbidden in Phase A
Do NOT create packaging deliverables in Phase A: `ARTICLE.md`, `RESEARCH_PAPER.md`, `demo.py`, `PACKAGE.json`.

### Recursive Abduction / Thread Continuation (v19c)
If prior-cycle context is provided, treat it as a live research thread: refine
the hypotheses from the previous cycle, attempt to close open conjectures, and
produce three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures. If no prior context is
provided, still run a self-contained abductive loop: generate conjectures, test
them, and immediately spin off the most promising follow-up conjectures as
future directions.


            ## Hard Constraints
            1. Every theorem MUST be fully proved (0 sorries, no stubbed signatures).
            2. No circular proofs (a theorem must never reference itself directly or transitively in its proof).
            3. No trivial results (e.g. `True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `native_decide`-only).
            4. All files must be self-contained and compilable with Lean 4 (mathlib4 v4.28.0).
            5. Build directly on existing catalog definitions — do not re-invent.

            ## Output Requirements
            Return ONLY:
            1. `.lean` files in `Catalog/Novelty/` with complete formal proofs.
            2. `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` with 3–5 concrete, falsifiable conjectures derived from your findings.
            3. `SELF_EVALUATION.json` with your honest self-assessment of the research:
               {
                 "quality_score": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "proof_depth": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "novelty": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "grade": "world_class" | "substantial" | "partial" | "shallow" | "trivial",
                 "rationale": "<2-3 sentence justification of grade and mathematical significance>"
               }

            Focus all compute budget on proving theorems.


### Computational Evidence Stage (Recommended)

Before writing the formal Lean 4 proof, you are strongly encouraged to produce
computational evidence for the claim. Create a file named `ComputationalEvidence.md`
in the project directory with:

1. **Small-case calculations** — compute the first several instances of the object/conjecture.
2. **OEIS search results** — if a sequence appears, note its OEIS ID and first terms.
3. **Counterexample hunt** — test the universal claim on a representative sample; report any counterexample found.
4. **Plots or tables** — include any relevant visual/numerical data.

If you choose to skip this stage, you MUST explicitly justify why computational
evidence is unnecessary or infeasible in a `SkipEvidenceJustification.md` file.

concept.title: Sturmian Structure of the Argmax Staircase
concept.concept_description:
The upper bracketing degree of the binomial weights is ⌊(n+1)α⌋ with α = p/(p+q), a Beatty sequence. The conjecture is that the increment word of the argmax staircase is the Sturmian word of slope α, so the combinatorics of binomial peaks is the combinatorics of a circle rotation.

The word w n = lastArgmax (n+1) - lastArgmax n ∈ {0,1} is the Sturmian/Beatty word of slope p/(p+q); in particular it is balanced and has exactly n+1 factors of length n when α is irrational.

Identify lastArgmax with ⌊(n+1)α⌋ (already proved) and connect to mathlib's Beatty sequence API; verify balance numerically for several α.

Transfers the full Sturmian toolkit (continued fractions, three-distance theorem) to statements about binomial peaks.

The staircase carries extra arithmetic from the +1 shift and is not literally Sturmian, which itself is a precise structural statement.
